speaker_role: former admissions officer (former Brown University undergraduate admissions officer; now works in private school/independent college counseling)
commercial_incentive: yes - speaker works in paid private-school and independent admissions counseling; podcast is produced by an education consultancy (referenced as 'A&J Education' / 'n education')
key_insights: Applications at Brown were read on a rolling basis as they arrived rather than batched until the deadline, with volume peaking heavily after the November 1 early decision deadline through March.

Brown scored each application section (academic profile, letters of recommendation, activity profile) on a 1-5 scale, producing a composite score used to determine strong consideration, but this was based on a full, complete read rather than an algorithm or AI.

Students are evaluated in the context of their specific high school and region; standardized test scores and GPA are compared against that school's own profile/average rather than judged in isolation.

Attempts to 'game' the system, such as transferring to a different high school late in the process to boost class rank, are usually easily identified by admissions officers familiar with regional feeder schools.

At elite schools, initial scoring narrows a large pool of similarly outstanding students; the supplemental 'why this school' essay becomes a key differentiator, and final admit decisions go through a committee vote rather than resting with one reader.

Recommends an activity profile shaped like a 'vase': a broad base of varied engagement combined with one clear area of focused depth/expertise (research, projects, or a distinctive skill), rather than either pure breadth or a single narrow spike.

When evaluating advantaged opportunities (expensive summer programs, family-connected internships), the speaker says admissions focuses on what the student learned/did with the opportunity rather than penalizing access advantages outright.

Selective colleges reject some very strong applicants specifically because they judge the student unlikely to enroll and prefer to protect yield/fit rather than 'waste' an offer, which the speaker says explains many puzzling admissions outcomes.

Rankings are a poor proxy for fit: a school's overall rank may not reflect strength in a specific department, and curriculum structure (e.g., Brown/Amherst's open curriculum vs. a highly structured program) matters for whether a student will succeed there.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Brown University scored application sections on a 1-5 point scale (per the speaker, former Brown admissions officer)
notable_or_distinctive: Directly names and explains the internal 1-5 scoring rubric used at a specific Ivy League admissions office, including how school-context comparison works, which is more procedurally specific than most general admissions-myths content.
reliability_notes: Speaker has verifiable former-admissions-officer credentials at one institution (Brown), and generalizes from that single institution's practices (and current work with a self-selected private-counseling clientele) to 'elite schools' broadly; presented within a podcast tied to a paid education consultancy.
